crux.for_the_english: Keep the vision unlocated, unbelabored, and in the same plain diction as the supper. Do not call it heaven, death, old age, a daydream, or a premonition, and do not make the three figures explicitly the couple grown old. Let abstract nouns repeat rather than finding synonyms for them: quiet/rest/peace, nostalgia or fond remembrance, forgiveness, sadness, suffering, weariness. The English will want to vary, explain, and lift these into lyricism; resist that ennoblement.
crux.point: The story stands or falls on a change of temporal distance inside an ordinary mouthful, and on that change not being explained. A badly cooked potato — hard, gritty, tasteless, “as if frozen” — detaches the young mother from the table and lets the three years of her marriage look first like a whole lifetime already lived and then like something seen from an immensely distant future, when everything in life, good and evil, grief, anger, trouble, joy, will have passed and turned into fond remembrance and forgiveness in an unending quiet. She even sighs as if she were already old, already looking back; then the shock of the arithmetic returns: it is only three years. The hope that carries the last page is not that life will improve, or that poverty will end, but that a day exists — after long life, long sadness, long suffering — from which even these days will be held in that same remembrance and forgiveness. The vision must stay as unparaphrasable in English as it is in Japanese: perhaps old age, perhaps death, perhaps simply time itself, told as a dim picture of “three people” gathered head to head over an endless story, smiling, unmoving, wrapped in quiet.
crux.why: If that distance is clarified into a consolation, a religious promise, or a young wife's determined optimism, the ending collapses into a moral about enduring hardship. The text's force is that she comes back to 'let us work' and 'let us get up early tomorrow' holding something she herself half-says she does not understand, and that the husband can only meet it partway ('…もう少しの間だ').

crux.for_the_english: Domestic detail and visionary abstraction must be allowed the same weight and the same vocabulary. Keep the potato literal and faintly unpleasant before it is anything else; keep steam, bowls hidden under the table, the spoon banged down, rice pushed into two mouths at once, breastfeeding at the end, exactly as physical as they are. Do not cut or compress the long domestic opening to 'get to' the meditation, and do not signal the meditation as the important part by changing the music when it arrives.
crux.point: The second crux is that the revelation happens inside, and is continuously interrupted by, an unremarkable supper. Nearly a third of the text is the baby: plump, gripping the table, snatching at everything, so that bowls and pots are moved underneath, leaving only her spoon and small plate; parents smiling helplessly, feeding her and themselves in snatches, forgetting the storm in the noise. The mother's trance is broken twice by the husband's plain 'why are you so quiet?', and what finally answers it is not a confession of the vision but the banal, startling fact: 'it really is only a little while since we married, isn't it.' The story ends not on the vision but on clearing the table, nursing the child asleep, and noticing the weather.
crux.why: A fluent draft will tidy this into an arc — happy family, dark thought, epiphany, renewed resolve — and in doing so will rationalise away what the text actually does, which is to let the eternal and the next morning's early rising sit side by side without commentary. The last line must be allowed to be only 'a storm, isn't it.'

open_questions.question: 「坊や」 is used repeatedly to and of the child, who is stated plainly in p2 to be a girl. Is this a period/familial generic endearment to be neutralised in English ('baby', 'little one'), a deliberate boyish pet name to be kept somehow, or an inconsistency to note? Keeping a literal equivalent risks making English readers misread the child's sex; neutralising loses a period usage.
open_questions.why_it_matters: The child's sex, age and boyish address are part of the period texture; mistranslating any one quietly falsifies the family.

open_questions.question: Who are the three quiet people in the dim picture, heads together over the endless story? The young family transposed into a distant future, an image of all humankind at the end of time, or an intentionally generic vision that should not be resolved even in pronoun and article choices? English will press for definiteness ('the three of them') where the Japanese can leave the figures suspended.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Deciding this decides whether the vision is domestic prophecy or a vision of the whole of life passing, and the text seems to want the second reading to grow out of the first without replacing it.

open_questions.question: Is the coming day of remembrance, forgiveness and 'rest like night' located in old age, after death, or deliberately in neither? Relatedly, how far should '安息' be allowed to sound religious in English ('rest', 'repose', 'peace') without importing a doctrine the text never states?
open_questions.why_it_matters: The consolation's vagueness is its character; too Christian a word makes it a belief, too secular a word makes it mere retirement.

data.reading:
Begin with the frame, because the text does: outside the door, a storm; inside, under a dim lamp hanging by the wall of a narrow room, a young couple — still really young, no wrinkles yet, but with a deep, drowsy weariness already in his hollowed, gentle eyes and in her dark hair and slight shoulders — getting supper with their plump baby daughter. The storm is heard again only twice: once, quietly, in the middle of the mother's silence, and once in the husband's final whisper, when the child has fallen asleep at the breast and everything has gone still. Between those hearings it is forgotten, drowned by the happy bustle of feeding the child. That arc of sound — storm, forgetting, storm — should remain an arc of sound, not be turned into symbolism or pathetic fallacy; the weather does not mirror anyone's feelings, it simply goes on outside, unheard and then heard.

The narration begins with the couple together, their weariness shared, both of them watching the child with all their eyes; then, by way of the potato, it narrows almost imperceptibly into the mother, and for the rest of the text we are mostly inside her drifting attention, which slides — the text keeps saying ふと, いつか, いつとなく, 'before she knew it', 'at some point', 'suddenly' — rather than deciding anything. Who is seeing, and when, is often left soft in the Japanese, and that softness is the medium of the story: present supper, remembered three years, and imagined far future keep soaking into one another, so that she can feel 'as if she had quite grown old' over a life that turns out to have lasted three years. Do not firm these transitions up with signposts ('she realised', 'she imagined', 'years later she would…'). Likewise her silence must stay silence: the husband asks twice why she is quiet, she starts, cannot say it in one breath, smiles 'as if with fond remembrance', and produces only the fact about the three years and, later, the resolve to work. The vision is never reported to him, and the English must not let her reported speech or his answers imply that it has been.

The register is Taishō literary prose in historical kana, gentle and slightly formal, but in its own terms plain: the power is in accumulation and recurrence, not in striking phrases. Watch the network of repeated words, which a fluent model will instinctively vary into elegance: 静か (quiet), 遠い (far, distant), 黙って (silently, without speaking), 微笑/笑ひ (the smiles that keep overflowing the parents' faces and fill the faces in the vision), 疲れ・悲しみ・苦しみ (weariness, sadness, suffering, returning in list after list, at the table, in memory, in the vision, in her rallying questions), なつかしみ and 許し (fond remembrance and forgiveness, the paired nouns on which the whole vision turns), 安らかさ (a quiet restfulness that describes the evening, the vision, and the mother's final manner of speaking). These repetitions are the connective tissue; destroying them destroys the text. The sentences should be allowed to run long and loop with 'and… and…' where the Japanese does, and to pool into those slow lists of everything life contains. Shortening them into crisp modern periods would rationalise a consciousness that experiences time as one long, unbroken telling.

Voice and address carry period and class quietly: a poor young household, beef and onions and carrots and potatoes stewed in a dark blue pot, rice steaming from an aluminium pan, things cleared under the table. No ennoblement of the food, no picturesque poverty, and no coarsening either; the husband's speech is rough-edged and warm (「きかない奴だな」, 「さうだなァ」, 「俺たち」), the wife's soft and feminine in the period manner (「…ませんのね」), and the difference between them should be audible in English without dialect costume or archaism. The baby is called 坊や throughout, though she is a girl; see the open questions. What the parents feel for her is rendered physically — the cheek pinched between finger and thumb, rice got into her small red mouth in the gaps of feeding themselves — and the text's tenderness lies in not naming it more grandly than that.

The likely fluent failures are: smoothing the mother's meditation into a tidy inspirational arc with a lesson; making the husband a foil who 'doesn't understand' (he is tired too, he has laboured too, and his 'it won't be much longer' is his own version of the same hope, not a failure of sympathy); explaining the potato; translating the vision's abstractions into richer, more varied, more consoling language than the text permits itself; and tidying away the ending's refusal to end — the table half-cleared, the child asleep mid-feed, a man standing still and murmuring about the weather.
data.say: Reading for Shiraki Shizu's 「晩餐」 (1917): a young, poor couple, worn down after only three years of marriage, eat supper with their baby in a storm. From one mouthful of bad potato the mother drifts into a vision in which their whole life, seen from an immense distance, will turn into fond remembrance and forgiveness; the story stands or falls on keeping that vision as unexplained, repetitive and domestic as the text leaves it — and below are the unresolved questions and the voice I recommend.

voice_takes.label: a
voice_takes.line: Plain, quiet, slightly formal; repetitions and long looping sentences kept, diction kept low so the vision and the potato share one voice. (Recommended.)

voice_takes.label: b
voice_takes.line: Warmer and more lyrical, letting the mother's interior passages rise in cadence above the supper scenes.

voice_takes.label: c
voice_takes.line: Drier and sparser, shorter sentences and modern plainness, letting the strangeness come only from the time-shift itself.
